sections.title: Warm-up
sections.prompt: Read the questions aloud with a rising voice at the end. Do not add an English “do”.
sections.lede: German questions are built with word order, not with an extra helping verb.

sections.title: Learning objectives
sections.lede: By the end of this lesson you will be able to ask for information and answer simple questions.

sections.title: The big picture
sections.lede: German has two question patterns: one starts with a question word, the other starts with the verb.

blocks.text: A W-question asks for information and begins with a question word such as wer, was, wo, wann, wie or warum. A yes/no question asks for a confirmation and begins with the conjugated verb. Both patterns are short, and both keep the verb in a fixed place.
Wo wohnst du? Wohnst du in Berlin?
blocks.en: Where do you live? Do you live in Berlin?

items: W-question: question word + verb + subject. Wo wohnst du?
Yes/no question: verb + subject + rest. Wohnst du in Berlin?
There is no German equivalent of “do”. The main verb moves to the front instead.
Answers can be short: Ja. / Nein. / In Berlin. / Aus Brasilien.

blocks.title: The polite form
blocks.text: With Sie the verb ends in -en: Wo wohnen Sie? / Wohnen Sie in Berlin? The pattern stays exactly the same.

sections.title: Rules & patterns
sections.lede: Six question words cover most of what you need at A1.

items: wo asks about a place, wann about a time, warum about a reason.
woher asks about origin: Woher kommst du? wohin asks about direction: Wohin gehst du?
wie viel asks about an amount or a price: Wie viel kostet das?
The polite Sie form keeps the same order: Woher kommen Sie? / Kommen Sie aus Spanien?

blocks.title: Answering a negative question
blocks.text: If someone asks Wohnst du nicht in Berlin?, a simple Ja would be confusing. German uses Doch to correct the assumption: Doch, ich wohne in Berlin. It means “yes, I do”, against the negative question.

sections.title: Vocabulary
sections.lede: Four question words and two nouns for talking about questions themselves.

sections.title: Example sentences
sections.lede: Each question is followed by a natural short answer.

items.de: Wer ist das? — Das ist meine Lehrerin.
items.en: Who is that? — That is my teacher.

items.de: Was ist das? — Das ist ein Schlüssel.
items.en: What is that? — That is a key.
Where do you live? — In Berlin.
items.note: A short answer with the place is enough.

items.de: Wann beginnt der Kurs? — Um neun Uhr.
items.en: When does the course start? — At nine o'clock.

items.de: Warum lernst du Deutsch? — Weil ich in Berlin arbeite.
items.en: Why are you learning German? — Because I work in Berlin.
items.note: warum asks for a reason; the answer often starts with weil.

sections.title: Pronunciation
sections.lede: All German question words except wer and was begin with a v sound.

items.hint: Vair. The w is a v sound, and the e is open.
Voh. Round your lips for the o and keep it long.
Vahn. A short a, and the double n is held briefly.
va-ROOM. Stress the second syllable, with a long oo.
FRAH-guh. The g is soft, and the final e is a weak “uh”.

blocks.text: If you did not understand a question, Wie bitte? is the standard way to ask someone to repeat it. It is polite and works in shops, offices and classrooms. Entschuldigung at the start of a question makes it softer: Entschuldigung, wo ist der Bahnhof?

German yes/no questions are answered with Ja or Nein, and a negative question can be answered with Doch. That small word is very common in conversation: it confirms the positive fact against a negative assumption. There is no single English word for it, which is why it is worth learning as a fixed reply.

sections.title: Grammar spotlight
sections.heading: Two ways to ask, one verb position
sections.lede: The verb is the anchor: in second position after a question word, in first position in a yes/no question.

items: In a W-question the question word occupies position one, so the verb is still in position two.
In a yes/no question there is no question word, so the verb itself moves to position one.
The subject follows the verb in both patterns: wohnst du, wohnen Sie.
Do not use “do” or “does”. The German verb carries the question on its own.

rows: Nein, ich wohne nicht in Berlin.

sections.tip: Read a statement, then turn it into both question types: Du wohnst in Berlin. → Wo wohnst du? → Wohnst du in Berlin?

sections.title: Choose the right answer
sections.lede: Choose the question word that fits the answer.

exercises.explanation: wie asks “how”, and Wie heißt du? is the standard way to ask someone's name.

sections.title: Build the sentence
sections.lede: Question word, verb, subject — or verb, subject for a yes/no question.

exercises.explanation: The question word is first, the verb second, the subject third.
A yes/no question starts with the conjugated verb.
Wann is position one, beginnt is position two, and the subject follows.

sections.title: Speaking
sections.lede: Ask three questions to get to know a new classmate.
sections.prompt: Ask for a name, an origin and a reason for learning German. Then answer one of them yourself.

model.de: Wie heißt du? Woher kommst du? Warum lernst du Deutsch? — Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland studiere.
model.en: What is your name? Where do you come from? Why are you learning German? — I am learning German because I study in Germany.

tips: Start each question with the question word and keep the verb directly after it.
For a yes/no question, begin with the verb and let your voice rise at the end.
Record the three questions, then listen for the difference between wo, wann and warum.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.lede: Word order is the main source of errors in German questions.

items.why: In a W-question the verb comes immediately after the question word, before the subject.
A yes/no question starts with the verb. The statement order Du sprichst Deutsch is only a statement, or a question marked purely by intonation in casual speech.

items.wrong: Wer ist das? — Das ist ein Buch.
items.right: Was ist das? — Das ist ein Buch.
items.why: wer asks about people; was asks about things. A book is a thing.
wann asks about time, wo about place. Living somewhere is a place, so the question needs wo.
